subject: Connection pattern recommendation for EdgeWave private deployment: peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Alice Gomez <alice@edgewave.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>
Cc: netops@edgewave.com, Tom Li <tom.li@edgewave.com>
Date: Sun, 15 Nov 2026 16:22:00 -0800
Subject: Quick ask — recommended connection for our private deployment

Hi Rishi,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. We're finalizing the architecture for our private deployment (single-region, production workload) and trying to pick a single primary connectivity pattern: VPC Peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or site-to-site VPN.

High level constraints:
- We need predictable p99 latency for inference (goal: <40ms for most calls).
- Sensitive PII in transit, SOC2 requirements, and we may need to present the network design to auditors.
- EdgeWave prefers minimal changes to our VPC routing table and limited public exposure.
- We may want a low-cost fallback channel for failover.

Can you outline pros/cons and recommend what you typically advise for a customer like us? Also can you call out operational impacts (routing, NAT, egress IPs, cutover steps)? I've attached our initial network diagram and access requirements.

—Alice
Alice Gomez
Head of Cloud Ops | EdgeWave Systems
Attachments: edgewave-net-access-reqs.pdf
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Gomez <alice@edgewave.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 16 Nov 2026 09:40:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Quick ask — recommended connection for our private deployment

Alice — thanks for the clear summary and the diagram. High level recommendation up front: for the constraints you listed I suggest a primary PrivateLink (interface endpoint) deployment with a peering-style fallback (short-lived S2S VPN) for cross-region/backstop traffic.

Why PrivateLink first?
- Minimal blast radius: interface endpoints keep the dataplane connection into Redwood in customer VPCs without broad route propagation. That aligns with your auditors' desire for limited routing exposure.
- Stable egress/IPs: outbound calls to Redwood come from an endpoint; simplifies allowlists and egress control.
- Lower attack surface: no route table changes that allow broader subnet-to-subnet reachability.
- Performance: for single-AZ private endpoints within the same region p99 is generally comparable to peering for short inference flows (we've seen p99 within your target for similar customers), and you avoid some NAT traversal jitter.

Tradeoffs / operational notes:
- Interface endpoints require per-AZ ENIs; you'll need to provision endpoint subnets in each AZ you expect traffic from. That adds some operational work and a modest hourly cost.
- DNS: PrivateLink needs split-horizon DNS (you'll point our service hostname to the interface endpoint IPs). We can provide a Route53 conditional-forwarder template or CNAME guidance if you run your own DNS.
- Quotas: some clouds limit ENIs per account/AZ; include a quota check in your pre-provisioning checklist.

Why keep a peering/VPN fallback?
- Peering gives lower operational overhead if you later want full L3 reachability for multiple microservices, but it exposes more of your subnet map to Redwood which you said you prefer to avoid.
- An S2S VPN as a failover (BGP or static routes) provides an out-of-band path we can bring up quickly during the endpoint/permission/route cutover. It also helps for cross-region replication scenarios where PrivateLink is region-scoped.

Cutover sketch (high level):
1) Quota + ENI check (EdgeWave cloud account).
2) Provision interface endpoints in target AZs + update endpoint subnets.
3) Update internal DNS to resolve redwood-api.edgewave.example -> endpoint IPs (test using dig / curl with override).
4) Deploy a canary app talker (small set of calls) to validate p99 and auth flows.
5) Create S2S VPN profile (pre-shared key / BGP) but keep it disabled in production routing until cutover window.
6) Cutover traffic to PrivateLink, monitor latency/cost/err rates for 1–2 days.
7) If failures, flip to VPN fallback and rollback DNS.

Attachments we recommend I share: tailored route53 template, a short runbook for failover, and an endpoint provisioning checklist. I attached a quick SOC2 notes matrix and a network diagram for your reviewers.

Are you available Tuesday morning for a 30-min call to walk through the checklist? If helpful I'll loop in Connor to talk about VPN automation and Kimberly to call out quota/ENI limits.

—Rishi

Couple of follow-ups on ENI / routing details that we should validate before the call:

1) NAT & egress: if EdgeWave uses NAT gateways for outbound traffic, confirm whether your inference callers originate from private subnets behind NAT. PrivateLink avoids NAT for inbound to the endpoint but your app's outbound egress still matters for other upstream services.

2) IP address planning: PrivateLink ENIs consume IPs from the endpoint subnets. If you have tight IP space in those subnets we should either expand them or use smaller subnets dedicated to endpoints.

3) Firewall / security groups: you can lock down the endpoint ENIs to the minimum source ranges (CIDRs) of the caller subnets. For peering there's no SG boundary so you need route + NACL hygiene.

4) Observability: we recommend enabling VPC Flow Logs for the endpoint subnets and a short-term packet capture during canary traffic to validate handshake patterns (TLS / mTLS).

I can prepare a one-page checklist that maps each of the items above to the cutover steps Rishi listed. Connor — can you add a short blurb on how we automate VPN deployment (Terraform + BGP) and the expected time to bring a fallback route online?

—Kimberly
